description: Types, annotations, and why TypeScript exists — JavaScript with a seatbelt.

screens.body:
JavaScript lets you do anything — including things you didn't mean. Pass a string where a number belongs and JS shrugs; you only find out when your app breaks at 2 AM.

TypeScript is JavaScript plus types. You describe what each value should be, and TypeScript checks your code BEFORE it runs. Typos and wrong types become red squiggles in your editor instead of crashes in production.

options: Catches type mistakes before the code runs
check.question: What does TypeScript give you that plain JS doesn't?

screens.heading: Why TypeScript exists
screens.keyPoint: TypeScript catches type mistakes before your code runs.

screens.body:
A type annotation is a label after a colon that says what a value must be. The syntax is simple: name, colon, type.

If you try to assign the wrong kind of value, TypeScript refuses. Your editor shows the error the moment you type it — no need to run anything.

check.question: Which line correctly annotates a number?

screens.heading: Type annotations: name, colon, type
screens.keyPoint: name: type — TypeScript enforces it from then on.

screens.body:
The everyday types: string (text), number (any number — no separate int/float), boolean (true/false).

Arrays add square brackets: string[] means "an array of strings". And null and undefined are their own types too — TypeScript is strict about them, which saves you from the classic "cannot read property of undefined" crash.

check.question: The type for an array of strings is…

screens.heading: The everyday types
screens.keyPoint: string, number, boolean — and string[] for arrays of strings.

screens.body:
You don't have to annotate everything. TypeScript is smart: if you write let city = "Calgary", it infers the type is string and will still complain if you later assign a number.

Rule of thumb: annotate function parameters and return types (where mistakes hide), let inference handle simple variables. Less typing, same safety.

options: It figures out the type from the value
check.question: What does type inference do?

screens.heading: Type inference does the boring work
screens.keyPoint: Annotate function signatures; let inference handle the rest.

screens.body:
Here's the big mental model: TypeScript errors happen at BUILD time (when you write/compile), JavaScript errors happen at RUN time (when the user clicks).

Build-time errors are cheap — you see them in your editor, fix them in seconds. Run-time errors are expensive — they happen on someone's phone. TypeScript moves bugs from expensive to cheap.

options: Build time — before the code ever runs
Run time — when the user clicks
check.question: When do TypeScript type errors appear?

screens.heading: Compile-time vs run-time
screens.keyPoint: TS errors are cheap (build time); JS errors are expensive (run time).

screens.body:
TypeScript doesn't run in browsers — it compiles down to plain JavaScript first. The tool is called tsc, the TypeScript compiler.

In practice you rarely run tsc by hand. Your editor checks types live, and your build tool (Vite, Next.js) strips the types when bundling. The types are scaffolding: they guide you, then disappear.

options: It runs directly in the browser
It compiles down to plain JavaScript
It needs a special TypeScript browser
check.question: How does TypeScript code actually run?

code.snippet:
# display-only: the typical flow
npx tsc app.ts    # compiles…
# → app.js        # …to plain JavaScript

screens.heading: TypeScript becomes JavaScript
screens.keyPoint: Types are scaffolding: they guide you, then compile away.

screens.body:
The red squiggle is your friend, not your enemy. When TypeScript underlines something, read the message out loud — they're written in plain English: "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'."

Translation: "you gave me text, I wanted a number." Fix the value, squiggle gone. Every squiggle you fix is a bug your users never meet.

options: Read it — it tells you exactly what's wrong
check.question: A red squiggle appears. You…

screens.heading: Reading a TypeScript error
screens.keyPoint: Read the squiggle out loud — it tells you the fix.
